successors.note: Kauaʻi was a tributary domain of the Hawaiian Kingdom from April 1810 (Kaumualiʻi as governor) and was ruled directly after his death on 26 May 1824.

rulers.name: Kamakahelei
rulers.title: ruling chiefess
rulers.note: Infobox: reign 1770-1794, predecessor Peleʻioholani; her husband Kāʻeokūlani (killed 12 December 1794) together with her united Niʻihau and Kauaʻi (paraphrased), undated.

rulers.name: Kaumualiʻi
rulers.title: aliʻi nui, from 1810 royal governor of Kauaʻi
rulers.note: The lead says he reigned 1794 to 1810, the succession table 1795-1810; royal governor 1810-1824; died 26 May 1824.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no Kauaʻi row). The Kaumualiʻi page makes him 'the last independent aliʻi nui of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau' and the kingdom 'Kauaʻi and Niʻihau'; the island has about 1,430 km2 (not on the pages) against about 1,000 km2 of land cells for the stand-in. From April 1810 the same land is a tributary domain of the Hawaiian Kingdom (recorded as a vassal tint by kingdom-of-hawai-i); the dossier runs to Kaumualiʻi's death in 1824 so that the vassal tint has a land to cover. From July to December 1794 Kāʻeokūlani also held Maui and Molokaʻi (ledger).

ledger.note: 1770: Kamakahelei is ruling chiefess of Kauaʻi. The page says she 'was the ruling chiefess of Kauaʻi from 1770 - 1794' (infobox reign 1770-1794, predecessor Peleʻioholani) and that she and Kāʻeokūlani united Niʻihau and Kauaʻi (paraphrased, undated). The extent of her realm (Kauaʻi and Niʻihau) is the Kaumualiʻi page's.

1794: Kāʻeokūlani receives Maui and Molokaʻi. Kahekili II died in 1794 (July, Kahekili II page) and left Oʻahu to Kalanikūpule and Maui and Molokaʻi to Kāʻeokūlani, whom the Unification page's list of domains gives as holding Kauaʻi and, in 1794, Maui and Molokaʻi (paraphrased). Kāʻeokūlani was the husband of Kamakahelei, who died the same year.

1794: Kāʻeokūlani is killed and Maui and Molokaʻi pass to Kalanikūpule. 'Kāʻeokūlani was killed at the Battle of Kukiiahu on December 12, 1794'; the Unification page has the civil war end 'when Kalanikūpule killed Kāʻeokūlani', giving Kalanikūpule Maui and Molokaʻi, and starting a succession crisis on Kauaʻi that ended with Kaumualiʻi king.

1824: Kaumualiʻi dies and Kauaʻi passes under direct Hawaiian rule. He died 'on May 26, 1824'; 'After Kaumualiʻi's death in 1824,' his son Humehume 'attempted to reestablish the independence of Kauaʻi' and failed. Kauaʻi had been 'a tributary domain under Kingdom of Hawaiʻi' since 1810, when 'Kaumualiʻi met face to face with Kamehameha in Honolulu and negotiated a peaceful surrender' (in April, Unification page).

wars.name: Kamehameha's attempts on Kauaʻi
wars.outcome: The spring 1796 attempt lost many canoes in the Kaʻieʻie Waho channel and was abandoned after Nāmakehā's rebellion in Hilo (Kaumualiʻi page: a rebellion forced Kamehameha home); the second invasion was postponed in 1803-1804 after an epidemic on Oʻahu. Kauaʻi submitted peacefully in April 1810.
wars.note: The Kaumualiʻi page says Kamehameha 'tried again in 1803, but disease ravaged his armies'; no 1809 invasion is on either page.

certainty.note: Two islands: the coast is the border. The status changes in 1810 (tributary) and 1824 (direct rule), not the shape.

notes: A state Cliopatria lacks; named in the Hawaiian Kingdom dossier only as a string ('Kaumualiʻi (Kauaʻi and Niʻihau)'), whose vassal_start (1810) and vassal_end (1824) now have a land to cover. Not on any page opened: the Kauaʻi chiefdom before 1770 (Peleʻioholani, Kamakahelei's relation to him 'not certain'), whether Kauaʻi paid tribute to Maui, Kāʻeokūlani's earlier conflicts (the Kamakahelei page is silent on 1780s invasions), the Russian forts of 1816-1817 (Fort Alexander, Fort Barclay-de-Tolly; agreement signed 1816, Russians expelled 1817, Kaumualiʻi page) which carry no territorial event, the date of Humehume's revolt (August 1824 is not on the page). The Hawaii dossier gives the vassal end and the gain at May 1824. The kingdom has no known capital; Holoholokū Heiau at Wailua is only Kaumualiʻi's birthplace. Region names: the Lihue 100 km stand-in is the one the Hawaiian Kingdom dossier uses (gazetteer_names_needed: Kauaʻi, Niʻihau).
